blocks.text: A nurse gives an intramuscular injection into the buttock of a patient. Placed a few centimetres too low and medially, the needle can strike the sciatic nerve and leave the patient with a painful, weak leg. The rule about where to give the injection is a direct application of the anatomy of the lumbosacral plexus.

blocks.markdown: The nerves of the lower limb arise from the **lumbar plexus** (spinal nerves L1 to L4) and the **sacral plexus** (L4, L5 and S1 to S4). As in the upper limb, the anterior rami combine and exchange fibres so that each named nerve carries fibres from several segments. The lumbar plexus supplies the anterior and medial thigh; the sacral plexus supplies the gluteal region, the posterior thigh, and everything below the knee.

blocks.title: Lumbar plexus
blocks.text: A network formed within the substance of psoas major from the anterior rami of L1 to L4 (with a contribution from T12 in some individuals). Posterior divisions give the femoral nerve and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh; anterior divisions give the obturator nerve. Its branches emerge around the borders of psoas major or pass through it.

rows: Lower abdominal wall muscles and skin over the suprapubic and gluteal regions
Muscles of the lower abdominal wall; skin of the groin and anterior scrotum or labium
Cremaster muscle (genital branch); skin of the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch)
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps, sartorius, iliacus, pectineus); skin of the anterior thigh and medial leg (saphenous nerve)
Medial thigh muscles (adductors, gracilis, obturator externus); skin of the medial thigh
blocks.caption: Main branches of the lumbar plexus.

blocks.markdown: **Sacral plexus.** The sacral plexus lies on the posterior wall of the pelvis, on piriformis. It is formed from the **lumbosacral trunk** (L4 and L5, which descends over the pelvic brim to join) and the anterior rami of **S1 to S4**. Its branches mostly leave the pelvis through the **greater sciatic foramen**. They include the **superior gluteal nerve** (L4-S1, which exits above piriformis), the **inferior gluteal nerve** (L5-S2, below piriformis), the **sciatic nerve** (L4-S3), the **posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh** (S1-S3), and the **pudendal nerve** (S2-S4, which supplies the perineum), together with nerves to piriformis, obturator internus and quadratus femoris.

rows: Exits above piriformis; gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae
Exits below piriformis; hamstrings, adductor magnus (hamstring part) and all muscles below the knee
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Skin of the posterior thigh and lower buttock
blocks.caption: Main branches of the sacral plexus.

blocks.title: The sciatic nerve
blocks.text: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. It has two parts bound in a common sheath: the tibial nerve (from the anterior divisions of the plexus) and the common fibular nerve (from the posterior divisions). It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, passes deep to gluteus maximus over the obturator internus, gemelli and quadratus femoris, runs down the back of the thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris, and usually divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves at the upper part of the popliteal fossa. The level of division is variable, and in some people it occurs higher.

blocks.title: Course of the sciatic nerve
blocks.prompt: List, in order, the key points along the course of the sciatic nerve from the pelvis to the knee.

steps.text: It begins in the pelvis from the sacral plexus (L4 to S3) and leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.
In the gluteal region it lies deep to gluteus maximus, midway between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity, resting on the obturator internus, gemelli and quadratus femoris.
It descends into the posterior thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris, supplying the hamstrings.
At or above the popliteal fossa it divides into the tibial nerve and the common fibular nerve.

blocks.answer: Greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), gluteal region, posterior thigh, then division into tibial and common fibular nerves at about the popliteal fossa.

blocks.markdown: **Gluteal intramuscular injections.** Many drugs are given into the gluteal muscles, which are large and well vascularised. The buttock is divided into four quadrants by a vertical line through the gluteal cleft and a horizontal line across the middle of the buttock. The **upper outer (superolateral) quadrant** is the safe site. This is because the **sciatic nerve** lies in the lower medial part of the buttock (deep, in the inferomedial quadrant), and the **superior gluteal vessels and nerve** and the **inferior gluteal and pudendal structures** occupy the medial quadrants. An injection into the lower medial area risks sciatic nerve injury, which can cause a painful paralysis of the muscles of the leg and foot and loss of sensation below the knee.

blocks.title: Choosing the injection site
blocks.prompt: A nurse divides the buttock into four quadrants. Which is the safe quadrant for gluteal intramuscular injection and why are the others avoided?

steps.text: Locate the sciatic nerve: it lies in the lower medial (inferomedial) quadrant.
The upper medial quadrant contains the superior gluteal vessels and nerve close to the sciatic notch.
The lower lateral quadrant is thin and lies close to the path of the sciatic nerve as it descends, so it is not the preferred site.
Therefore the thick gluteal muscle in the upper outer quadrant is the safe site.

blocks.answer: The upper outer quadrant, which avoids the sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels and nerves.

items: Lumbar plexus: L1-L4, formed within psoas major; main nerves are femoral (L2-L4) and obturator (L2-L4).
Sacral plexus: L4-S4; main nerves are superior and inferior gluteal, sciatic, pudendal and posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh.
Sciatic nerve (L4-S3): tibial part and common fibular part; leaves via the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.
Safe site for gluteal injection: upper outer quadrant.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the foramina
blocks.text: The sciatic nerve and the superior and inferior gluteal nerves leave through the greater sciatic foramen. The superior gluteal nerve exits above piriformis, while the sciatic and inferior gluteal nerves exit below it. The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the tendon of obturator internus and the pudendal nerve as it re-enters the perineum.

points: The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) lies in psoas major and gives the femoral and obturator nerves (both L2-L4); the sacral plexus (L4-S4) lies on piriformis and gives gluteal, sciatic and pudendal nerves.
The sciatic nerve (L4-S3) leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, runs through the gluteal region and posterior thigh, and divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
The upper outer quadrant of the buttock is used for injections to avoid the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels and nerves.

questions.stem: In which muscle is the lumbar plexus formed?

distractorRationale.b: Piriformis is the muscle on which the sacral plexus lies.
distractorRationale.c: Gluteus maximus covers the gluteal region.
distractorRationale.d: Quadratus femoris lies deep in the gluteal region.

questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus lies within the substance of psoas major, derived from the anterior rami of L1 to L4. Its branches emerge from the borders of the muscle or pass through it.

questions.stem: Which are the roots of the femoral nerve?

distractorRationale.b: L4 to S1 forms the superior gluteal nerve.
distractorRationale.c: S2 to S4 forms the pudendal nerve.
distractorRationale.d: T12 and L1 contribute to iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

questions.explanation: The femoral nerve is formed from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It supplies the anterior thigh muscles.

questions.stem: Through which opening and relative to which muscle does the sciatic nerve leave the pelvis?

options.text: Lesser sciatic foramen, below obturator internus

distractorRationale.b: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels exit above piriformis.
distractorRationale.c: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits obturator internus tendon and the pudendal nerve.
distractorRationale.d: The obturator canal transmits the obturator nerve.

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve passes through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis into the gluteal region. The superior gluteal vessels and nerve exit above the muscle.

questions.stem: The sciatic nerve divides into which two nerves?

options.text: Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve
Superior gluteal nerve and inferior gluteal nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve

distractorRationale.b: These are branches of the lumbar plexus.
distractorRationale.c: These are separate branches of the sacral plexus.
distractorRationale.d: These are sensory branches of the femoral and tibial nerves.

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve is a composite of the tibial nerve (anterior divisions) and the common fibular nerve (posterior divisions). They usually separate at the upper part of the popliteal fossa.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give an intramuscular injection into the gluteal region. Which site is safest, and why?

options.text: Upper outer quadrant, because it avoids the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels and nerves
Lower medial quadrant, because the muscle is thickest there
Upper medial quadrant, because it is close to the sacrum
Lower outer quadrant, because it overlies the femoral nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Upper outer quadrant, because it avoids the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels and nerves

distractorRationale.b: The sciatic nerve lies in the lower medial area.
distractorRationale.c: The superior gluteal vessels and nerve lie near the upper medial region.
distractorRationale.d: The femoral nerve is in the anterior thigh, not the buttock.

questions.explanation: The upper outer quadrant lies over the thick gluteus medius and gluteus maximus and is away from the sciatic nerve in the inferomedial region. It also avoids the superior gluteal and other neurovascular structures near the medial side.

questions.stem: Which nerve exits the pelvis above piriformis and supplies gluteus medius and minimus?

distractorRationale.b: The inferior gluteal nerve exits below piriformis and supplies gluteus maximus.
distractorRationale.c: The sciatic nerve exits below piriformis.
distractorRationale.d: The pudendal nerve exits below piriformis and supplies the perineum.

questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) passes above piriformis and supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. This is the nerve whose injury causes the Trendelenburg sign.

questions.stem: True or false: the sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen.

distractorRationale.a: The sciatic nerve passes through the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon and the pudendal nerve.

questions.stem: Describe the course of the sciatic nerve from the pelvis to the popliteal fossa, including its roots and its division.
markingGuide: Roots L4, L5, S1, S2 and S3 (sacral plexus).
Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.
Passes deep to gluteus maximus, over obturator internus, gemelli and quadratus femoris.
Descends in the posterior thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris.
Divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves, usually at the upper popliteal fossa.
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve is two nerves bound in a sheath, which usually divide at the popliteal fossa, although the level is variable. Knowing the course explains the risk of injury from hip dislocation and badly placed injections.

questions.stem: Explain why the upper outer quadrant of the buttock is the safe site for gluteal intramuscular injection, and what could happen if the injection is given in the lower medial quadrant.
markingGuide: The buttock is divided into four quadrants.
Upper outer quadrant overlies thick gluteal muscle away from major neurovascular structures.
The sciatic nerve lies in the lower medial (inferomedial) region.
Superior gluteal vessels and nerve lie near the medial side and sciatic notch.
Injury to the sciatic nerve causes pain, weakness of the hamstrings and muscles below the knee, and sensory loss below the knee (except the medial leg).
questions.explanation: The safe site is chosen by the location of the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels. A needle that strikes the sciatic nerve may produce a lasting neurological deficit.
